source_text: Iam uero nemo est, qui non hoc quoque praetendat: omnia a deo instituta et homini attributa, sicut praedicamus, et utique bona, ut omnia boni auctoris; inter haec deputari uniuersa ista, ex quibus spectacula instruuntur, equum uerbi gratia et leonem et uires corporis et uocis suauitates; igitur neque alienum uideri posse neque inimicum deo, quod de conditione constet ipsius, neque cultoribus dei deputandum, quod ei non sit inimicum, quia nec alienum. plane et ipsae extructiones locorum, quod saxa, quod caementa, quod marmora, quod columnae dei res sunt, qui ea ad instrumentum terrae dedit; sed et ipsi actus sub caelo dei transiguntur. quam sapiens argumentatrix sibi uidetur ignorantia humana, praesertim, cum aliquid eiusmodi de gaudiis et de fructibus saeculi metuit amittere. plures denique inuenias, quos, magis periculum uoluptatis quam uitae auocet ab hac secta. nam mortem etiam stultus ut debitam non extimescit, uoluptatem etiam sapiens ut optatam non contemnit, cum alia non sit et stulto et sapienti uitae gratia nisi uoluptas. nemo negat, quia nemo ignorat, quod ultro natura suggerit, deum esse uniuersitatis conditorem eamque uniuer sitatem tam bonam quam homini mancipatam. sed quia non penitus deum norunt nisi naturali iure, non etiam familiari, de longinquo, non de proximo, necesse est ignorent, qualiter administrari aut iubeat aut prohibeat quae instituit, simul quae uis sit aemula ex aduerso adulterandis usibus diuinae conditionis, quia neque uoluntatem neque aduersarium noueris eius quem minus noueris. non ergo hoc solum respiciendum est, a quo, omnia sint instituta, sed a quo conuersa. ita enim apparebit, cui usui sint instituta, si appareat, cui non. multum interest inter corruptelam et integritatem, quia multum est inter institutorem et interpolatorem. ceterum omnes species malorum, quae etiam ethnici ut indubitata et prohibent et defendunt, ex operibus dei constant. uides homicidium ferro ueneno magicis deuinctionibus perfici: tam ferrum dei res est quam herbae, quam † angeli. numquid tamen in hominis necem auctor ista prouidit? atquin omnem homicidii speciem uno et principali praecepto interimit: non occides. proinde aurum aes argentum ebur lignum et quaecumque fabricandis idolis materia captatur quis in saeculo posuit nisi saeculi auctor deus? numquid tamen, ut] haec aduersus ipsum adorentur? atquin summa offensa penes illum idololatria. quid non dei est quod deum offendit? sed cum offendit, dei esse desiit, et cum desiit, offendit. ipse homo, omnium flagitiorum auctor, non tantum opus dei, uerum etiam imago est; et tamen et corpore et spiritu desciit a suo institutore. neque enimin oculos ad concupiscentiam sumpsimus et linguam ad maliloquium et aures ad exceptaculum maliloquii et gulam ad gulae crimen et uentrem ad gulae societatem et genitalia ad excessus impudicitiae et manus ad uim et gressus ad uagam uitam, aut spiritus ideo insitus corpori, ut insidiarum, ut fraudium, ut iniquitatium cogitatorium fieret. non opinor. nam si omnem malignitatem et si etiam malitiam exco gitatam deus exactor innocentiae odit, indubitate quaecumque condidit non in exitum operum constat condidisse quae damnatat, licet eadem opera per ea quae condidit administrentur, quando haec sit tota ratio damnationis, pertuersa administratio conditionis a conditis. nos igitur, qui domino cognito etiam aemulum eius inspeximus, qui institutore comperto et interpolatorem una deprehendimus, nec mirari neque dubitare oportet: cum ipsum hominem, opus et imaginem dei, totius uniuersitatis possessorem, illa uis interpolatoris et aemulatoris angeli ab initio de integritate deiecerit, uniuersam substantiam eius pariter cum ipso integritati institutam pariterer cum ipso in peruersitatem demutauit aduersus institutorem, ut, quam doluerat homini concessam, non sibi, in ea ipsa et hominem reum deo faceret et suam dominationem collocaret.
thought_title: God made all things, but the devil corrupted their uses
orientation: Tertullian is answering the pagan objection that since God created everything used in the shows, the shows cannot be alien or hostile to God.
pass_a_gloss: But now there is no one who does not also put forward this: all things were instituted by God and assigned to man, as we proclaim, and certainly good, as all things of a good author; among these are reckoned all those things from which shows are constructed, a horse for example and a lion and the strengths of the body and the sweetnesses of the voice; therefore it can seem neither alien nor hostile to God, because it consists of his own creation, nor should it be reckoned to the worshipers of God, because it is not hostile to him, since it is not alien. Certainly also the very structures of the places, because the stones, because the cement, because the marbles, because the columns are things of God, who gave them for the equipment of the earth; but also the very performances are carried on under the sky of God. How wise an arguer human ignorance seems to itself, especially when it fears to lose something of this sort from the joys and from the fruits of the world. More numerous finally you may find whom the danger of pleasure rather than of life calls away from this sect. For even a fool does not fear death as something owed, even a wise man does not despise pleasure as something desired, since there is no other grace of life for both the fool and the wise man except pleasure. No one denies, because no one is ignorant, what nature suggests of its own accord, that God is the founder of the universe and that this universe is as good as it is handed over to man. But because they do not know God deeply except by natural law, not also by intimate law, from afar, not from nearby, it is necessary that they be ignorant how he orders or forbids the things he instituted to be administered, and at the same time what hostile force there is from the opposite side for adulterating the uses of the divine creation, because you would know neither the will nor the adversary of him whom you know less. Therefore not this alone must be looked at, by whom all things were instituted, but by whom they were perverted. For thus it will appear for what use they were instituted, if it appears for what use they were not. There is much difference between corruption and integrity, because there is much between the institutor and the interpolator. For the rest, all kinds of evils, which even the pagans both prohibit and defend as undoubted, consist of the works of God. You see homicide accomplished by iron, by poison, by magic bindings: iron is as much a thing of God as herbs, as the angels. Did the author nevertheless provide these things for the killing of man? But he destroys every kind of homicide with one and principal precept: you shall not kill. Likewise gold, bronze, silver, ivory, wood, and whatever material is sought for fabricating idols, who placed it in the world except God the author of the world? Did he nevertheless provide that these things be worshiped against himself? But idolatry is the highest offense with him. What is not of God that offends God? But when it offends, it ceases to be of God, and when it ceases, it offends. Man himself, the author of all outrages, is not only the work of God, but even his image; and yet he has fallen away from his institutor both in body and in spirit. For neither did we receive eyes for desire and the tongue for evil speaking and the ears for the receptacle of evil speaking and the throat for the crime of the throat and the belly for the partnership of the throat and the genitals for the excesses of unchastity and the hands for violence and the feet for a wandering life, or was the spirit for this reason placed in the body, that it should become a deviser of plots, of frauds, of iniquities. I do not think so. For if God, the exactor of innocence, hates all malignity and even all thought-out malice, undoubtedly whatever things he created he did not create for the destruction of the works which he condemns, although the same works are administered through the things which he created, since this is the whole reason of condemnation, the perverse administration of the creation by the created things. We therefore, who having known the Lord have also looked upon his rival, who having discovered the institutor have also caught the interpolator at the same time, ought neither to wonder nor to doubt: since that force of the interpolator and rival angel cast down from integrity from the beginning man himself, the work and image of God, the possessor of the whole universe, it changed the whole substance of his creation, instituted for integrity together with him, together with him into perversity against the institutor, so that in that very creation which it had grieved was granted to man, not to itself, it might both make man guilty before God and establish its own dominion.

choices.why: Keeps the legal/editorial metaphor of one who tampers with or corrupts an original text or work, matching Tertullian's contrast with institutor.
Preserves the active enmity and rivalry of the devil against God, not just abstract opposition.
Keeps the metaphor of adulteration, mixing a pure thing with something foreign to corrupt it, which fits Tertullian's argument about perverting creation.
Mancipatio is a formal transfer of ownership; 'handed over' conveys the legal transfer of creation to man without the technical Roman term.
Exactor is a tax-collector or enforcer; keeping it shows God as one who demands and enforces innocence, not merely loves it.
Deuinctio is a binding or tying up; 'bindings' preserves the concrete magical practice of binding spells.

pass_b_english: But now everyone puts forward this argument: all things were established by God and given to man, as we proclaim, and are certainly good, as all things of a good author are. Among these are reckoned all those things from which the shows are constructed—the horse, for example, and the lion, and the strength of bodies and the sweetness of voices. Therefore, they say, what consists of God's own creation can seem neither foreign nor hostile to God, nor should it be counted against God's worshippers, since it is not hostile to him, because it is not foreign.

And indeed the very structures of the places—the stones, the cement, the marbles, the columns—are God's things, for he gave them for the furnishing of the earth. But the very performances themselves take place under God's sky.

How wise an arguer human ignorance seems to itself, especially when it fears losing something of this kind from the joys and fruits of the world. In fact you will find more people whom the danger of pleasure rather than the danger of life calls away from this sect. For even a fool does not fear death as something owed, but even a wise man does not despise pleasure as something desired, since for both fool and wise man there is no other charm of life than pleasure.

No one denies, because no one is ignorant of what nature freely suggests, that God is the founder of the universe and that this universe is as good as it is handed over to man. But because they do not know God deeply except by natural law, not also by intimate acquaintance—from afar, not from near—they must necessarily be ignorant of how he commands or forbids the things he established to be administered, and at the same time what hostile rival force exists in opposition for adulterating the uses of the divine creation. For you cannot know either the will or the adversary of one whom you know less.

Therefore not only this must be considered: by whom all things were established, but also by whom they were perverted. For thus it will appear for what use they were established, if it appears for what use they were not. There is a great difference between corruption and integrity, because there is a great distance between the founder and the corrupter.

Besides, all the kinds of evils which even the pagans both forbid and defend as undoubted consist of the works of God. You see homicide accomplished by iron, by poison, by magic bindings: iron is as much God's thing as herbs are, as the angels are. Did the author, however, provide these things for the killing of man? On the contrary, he abolishes every kind of homicide with one primary command: "You shall not kill" (Exodus 20:13).

Likewise, who placed gold, bronze, silver, ivory, wood, and whatever material is sought for fabricating idols in the world except God, the author of the world? Did he, however, provide that these things should be worshipped against himself? On the contrary, idolatry is the highest offense in his sight. What is there that is not God's, that offends God? But when it offends, it ceases to be God's, and when it ceases, it offends.

Man himself, the author of all outrages, is not only the work of God but also his image; and yet he has fallen away from his founder in both body and spirit. For we did not receive eyes for desire, and a tongue for evil speaking, and ears for receiving evil speaking, and a throat for the crime of the throat, and a belly for the partnership of gluttony, and genitals for the excesses of unchastity, and hands for violence, and feet for a wandering life; nor was the spirit placed in the body to become a deviser of plots, of frauds, of iniquities. I do not think so.

For if God, the exactor of innocence, hates all malignity and even all devised malice, then undoubtedly whatever he created he did not create for the ruin of the works he condemns, even though those same works are administered through the things he created—since this is the whole reason for condemnation: the perverse use of creation by created things.

We, therefore, who have known the Lord and have also seen his adversary, who have discovered the founder and have likewise caught the corrupter, ought neither to wonder nor to doubt: since that force, the corrupter and rival angel, cast down man himself—the work and image of God, the possessor of the whole universe—from his integrity from the beginning, it likewise changed the entire substance of his creation, established for integrity together with him, into perversity together with him against the founder, so that in the very creation granted to man and not to himself, he might both make man guilty before God and establish his own dominion.
notes: The text contains '† angeli' with a dagger, indicating textual corruption or uncertainty at that point; the gloss renders it as 'the angels' but the reading is doubtful.
The text has 'ut]' with a bracket, suggesting a damaged or uncertain reading; the gloss renders the sense as 'that these things be worshiped'.

problems.quote: and a belly for the throat's partnership
problems.why: Latin says belly for the partnership of gluttony, not throat's partnership
problems.fix: and a belly for the partnership of gluttony
problems.ruling: gulae means gluttony/greed, not throat; mistranslates the sin being referenced.

edits.old: and a belly for the throat's partnership
edits.new: and a belly for the partnership of gluttony

fixed: Corrected 'throat's partnership' to 'partnership of gluttony' because the source 'gulae societatem' means partnership of gluttony, not of the throat.

problems.quote: Therefore this alone must not be considered: by whom all things were established, but by whom they were perverted.
problems.source_quote: non ergo hoc solum respiciendum est, a quo, omnia sint instituta, sed a quo conuersa.
problems.why: Latin says ‘not only this must be considered… but also who perverted them’; English reverses the negation, implying only the first part is to be ignored.
problems.fix: Therefore not only this must be considered: by whom all things were instituted, but also by whom they were perverted.
problems.ruling: Latin 'non solum...sed' = 'not only...but also'; English 'this alone must not be considered' wrongly reverses the required consideration.

edits.old: Therefore this alone must not be considered: by whom all things were established, but by whom they were perverted.
edits.new: Therefore not only this must be considered: by whom all things were established, but also by whom they were perverted.

fixed: The English reversed the negation of 'non ergo hoc solum respiciendum est... sed a quo conuersa'; corrected to 'not only... but also'.

problems.why: Syntax is tangled; 'which he had grieved was granted' does not parse as English.
problems.fix: Rewrite: 'so that in the very creation granted to man (not to himself), he might make man guilty before God'

edits.old: so that in the very creation which he had grieved was granted to man and not to himself, he might both make man guilty before God and establish his own dominion.

problems.fix: Punctuate as: 'What is there that is not God's, that offends God?'

fixed: The sentence 'What is not God's that offends God?' is ambiguous and reads as a statement; the source 'quid non dei est quod deum offendit?' is a rhetorical question meaning 'What is there that is not God's, that offends God?' Punctuated to clarify.

last_rejected.quote: On the contrary, he abolishes every kind of homicide with one primary command: You shall not kill (Exodus 20:13).
last_rejected.source_quote: atquin omnem homicidii speciem uno et principali praecepto interimit: non occides.
last_rejected.why: The source does not cite Exodus 20:13; the citation is an addition not in the Latin.
last_rejected.fix: On the contrary, he abolishes every kind of homicide with one primary command: non occides.
last_rejected.ruling: Scripture references are standard editorial additions, not translation errors; 'non occides' is correctly translated.

polish.changed: Clarified the sarcastic aside about human ignorance, marked the opponent's view on pleasure more naturally, replaced 'interpolator' with 'corrupter' throughout, and rendered 'administration' as 'use' where the moral sense requires it.

notes.quote: How wise an arguer human ignorance seems to itself
notes.why: Sarcastic comment on pagan argument; tone shift may confuse reader about whether Tertullian or opponent speaks.

notes.quote: since for both fool and wise man there is no other grace of life than pleasure
notes.why: Contradicts Tertullian's own view; seems to state opponent's view but not clearly marked, and 'grace of life' is odd for 'gratia' meaning 'charm/pleasure'.
notes.fix: Clarify as opponent's claim: 'for they say there is no other grace...'.

notes.quote: the perverse administration of creation by created things
notes.why: 'Administration' is too neutral; Latin likely means 'use' or 'management' in moral sense, but 'administration' sounds bureaucratic.
Used for devil/rival angel; 'interpolator' means textual insertor in English, not 'one who corrupts by insertion into creation'.
